vignette:
James is sixty-five years old, a tall, quiet man with a deliberate way of moving, as if he is always checking the ground in front of him before he takes the next step. He has worked at the same hardware store in a small coastal town for thirty-two years, stocking shelves and helping customers find the right size bolt or a length of chain. He is married to his wife, Esther, for forty-one years. He comes to therapy because, as he puts it, "Esther says I'm not the same man she married."

The story he tells begins on a Tuesday. It was the day the water came.

He had been at the store, in the back room, sorting through a delivery of PVC pipes. The rain had been falling for three days, a heavy, unrelenting gray curtain, but the town was used to rain. The radio chattered in the background, and the owner, a man named Frank, had been listening to the weather reports. "They're saying the river might top the levee," Frank had called out. James remembers thinking that was a thing people said, but never really believed. He kept sorting the pipes.

Then the sound came. It was not a roar, not exactly. It was a low, grinding hum, like the earth itself was groaning. The lights flickered and went out. The floor beneath him began to tremble, and then it was not trembling, it was moving. A wall of brown water, thick with debris, punched through the front of the store. It was not like a wave at the beach. It was like a solid wall of mud and wood and glass, and it was coming for him.

James does not remember climbing onto the metal shelving unit. He remembers the water rising, cold and gritty, up his legs, his waist, his chest. He remembers the sting of gasoline in the water, the splintered two-by-fours floating past like battering rams. He remembers holding onto the metal rack, his knuckles white, and watching Frank try to swim for the back door. He saw Frank's head go under, and he did not see it come back up. James held on for what he thinks was an hour. He held on while the water tried to pull him away. He held on while a car, upside down, floated past him. He held on while the world turned into a soup of brown and gray, and he screamed for help until his voice was gone.

The rescue came by boat, a man in an orange vest pulling him from the shelf. James’s legs were so weak he could not stand. He was taken to a high school gymnasium, wrapped in a damp blanket, and given a cup of cold soup. He did not sleep for three days.

That was four years ago.

Now, James cannot go near the hardware store. He tried, once, about a month after the flood. He walked to the end of the block, saw the plywood over the windows, the smell of mildew and mud still clinging to the air, and he vomited into the gutter. He has not been back. He is on disability now, but he cannot bring himself to say he is retired. "I'm just... waiting," he says.

His days are small. He wakes at 4:00 AM, heart pounding, sheets soaked with sweat. He sees the water in his sleep, feels the cold, hears the sound of Frank's head going under. He gets up, makes coffee, and sits in the dark living room, watching the street. He does not like the dark, but he cannot sleep with the lights on either. The light feels wrong, artificial, like it is hiding something.

He avoids the bathroom when it is raining. He cannot stand the sound of it against the window. He will stand in the kitchen, holding onto the counter, until the rain stops or Esther calls him back to himself. He has not driven over the bridge to the next town in two years. He says the water underneath it looks too close.

He is not angry, not loud. He is hollowed out. He will start a sentence about the garden and then stop, his eyes going distant. He cannot remember what he was going to say. He is afraid of the weather forecast. He checks it obsessively on his phone, ten, twenty times a day, and when he sees a high probability of rain, he feels a tightness in his chest that makes him want to crawl under the bed.

Esther tries. She holds his hand. She makes him tea. But he cannot tell her what he sees when he closes his eyes. He cannot tell her that the sound of the tap running in the sink makes him feel like he is drowning. He just sits in the dark living room, waiting for the next Tuesday, even though he knows it will not come. He knows the water is not coming. But his body does not know that. His body is still on that metal shelf, holding on.
